name: Transmit
tagline: Build a focused SFTP and object-storage client with bookmarks and transfer queue

pricing.notes: Sold as a one-time Mac licence.

tiers.name: Transmit 5 direct license
tiers.limits: 1 named user; install on every Mac that user owns or controls; 7-day unrestricted trial
tiers.notes: $45 one-time perpetual license for Transmit 5; a future major-version upgrade may be paid.

tiers.name: Transmit 5 Mac App Store annual
tiers.limits: 1 Apple Account; use on all Macs; major updates included while the subscription remains active
tiers.notes: $24.99 billed yearly; the App Store build stops working after expiry and has macOS sandbox limitations.

pricing.freeTierCaps: no free tier; 7-day full-featured unrestricted trial
pricing.billingTerms: one-time $45 direct license or annual-only $24.99 Mac App Store subscription; no monthly plan
pricing.hiddenCosts: The direct license may require a paid future major-version upgrade; the App Store edition stops working after expiry and cannot offer every direct-build integration.

verdictSummary: The core loop is small enough for a capable coding agent to produce a useful local version in one sitting. For Transmit, build a focused SFTP and object-storage client with bookmarks and transfer queue. The hard boundary is protocol compatibility, native polish, sync, security, and ongoing maintenance, plus os integration polish and maintenance.
coreLoopDIY: Build a focused macOS SFTP and object-storage client with bookmarks and a transfer queue, expose keyboard-first controls, and store settings locally.
requirements: only the permissions required by the selected feature
whatYouLose: protocol compatibility, native polish, sync, security, and ongoing maintenance
commercial support and rapid compatibility fixes
ongoingBurden: permissions, accessibility APIs, sandboxing, signing, notarization, OS regressions, updates, backups, and support
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Transmit because small utilities are technically reproducible, but customers pay for polish and immediate fixes when an OS update breaks a daily habit. The recurring cost buys permissions, accessibility APIs, sandboxing, signing, notarization, OS regressions, updates, backups, and support, not just the visible interface.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Transmit licence plan and a single-purpose local Mac app DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a personal replacement for Transmit in an empty repository.
Use Swift 6, SwiftUI, AppKit where necessary, SQLite, and the macOS Keychain; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: build a focused macOS SFTP and object-storage client with bookmarks and a transfer queue, expose keyboard-first controls, and store settings locally.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Create a menu-bar app with a searchable command window and global hotkey.
Implement only the primary feature and one settings screen instead of a plugin platform.
Request permissions just in time and explain why each is needed before opening System Settings.
Store configuration locally, support export or import, and never capture unrelated user content.
Add launch-at-login, update-check opt-in, diagnostics export, and a complete uninstall note.
Write unit tests for transformation logic and one UI test for the core keyboard workflow.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Deliberately leave out a third-party extension marketplace.
Deliberately leave out cloud accounts and cross-device sync.
Deliberately leave out broad automation that executes untrusted scripts.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
